summary: InspectApedia article answering whether special or biodegradable toilet paper is needed for homes on private septic systems. It concludes ordinary toilet tissue does not harm conventional tank-and-drainfield systems, that pumping on schedule matters more than paper choice, and that recycled-fiber tissue is recommended to spare forests. It also covers paper products that should never be flushed, and the note that septic additives are unnecessary.
one_line: Explains that ordinary toilet tissue is fine for septic systems and recommends recycled-fiber toilet paper to save trees.
key_facts: In a conventional septic system using a tank and drainfield, ordinary toilet tissue does not harm the septic system; the tissue remains in the septic tank, kept from flowing into the drainfield by septic tank baffles.
Lower-cost toilet tissues such as the Rite-Aid bathroom tissue perform better (break down faster and more completely) in septic tanks than some plush extra soft brands containing softening additives.
The article recommends toilet tissue made entirely or at least in part from recycled paper because manufacturing ultra-soft tissue requires new wood fibers from trees.
In February 2009 Greenpeace joined associations recommending against flushing trees down the toilet.

According to the Times article, 25% to 50% of the wood pulp used in toilet paper comes from tree farms in South America and the U.S., while the remaining 50% to 75% is cut from old growth forests including Canadian old growth timber.
Toilet paper made from recycled paper fibers uses less chlorine-based bleach, reducing groundwater pollution, and produces less landfill volume.
Dr. Allen Heskowitz, senior scientist and waste expert at the Natural Resource Defense Council, said "No forest of any kind should be used to make toilet paper."
Greenpeace recommends these toilet tissue brands as "most green": Green Forest, 365, April soft, Earth Friendly, Fiesta & Fiesta Green, Natural Value, Seventh Generation, Trader Joe's.
Marcal Corporation markets recycled paper-based toilet paper through Walgreens at prices below the "soft fluffy" brands.
The EPA's recommended recovered fiber content for commercial/industrial bathroom tissue is 20-60% post consumer fiber and 20-100% recovered fiber.
Paper towels, documents and newsprint should not be flushed into a septic system; most document papers, even newsprint, are slow to degrade in a septic tank.

Daniel Friedman's toilet tissue test, begun in 2009 and 2010, showed after eight years that the paper samples looked about the same, with the author stating that pumping the septic tank on time is more important than choice of toilet paper.
No septic system additives are needed for system maintenance, and some are illegal in some states; all are illegal in Canada, according to the article.
Where a chemical toilet is used, such as on a boat or recreational vehicle, special toilet tissue which dissolves rapidly is recommended.
